title.en: History: Evolution of Humans and Society - Prehistoric Period

text.en: Asha found a stone tool in a museum. "Who made this?" she asked.

History is the study of the human past. Prehistory refers to periods for which writing does not provide local evidence. Archaeologists often use Stone Age and Metal Age terms, with dates and subdivisions that vary by region. Early humans were hunter-gatherers who used stone tools and learned to make fire.
In the Neolithic age people began farming and settled in villages, and they made pottery and domesticated animals. Later the Chalcolithic, Bronze and Iron ages brought metal tools. Evidence comes from fossils, tools, cave paintings and burial sites, and sites such as Adichanallur in Tamil Nadu show early life in the south.
Human evolution involved related groups that branched and sometimes lived at the same time. Australopithecus and several Homo species are examples, and Homo sapiens is the species of all living humans. Sources of history are archaeological and literary, and archaeologists study the remains of the past.

A stone artefact can show patterns left by people in a place where there is no writing from that time. The shape and the location of the find both contribute evidence.
Historians ask questions about the human past. Archaeologists investigate material remains such as tools, building traces and pottery. Palaeoanthropologists study evidence for human evolution.

board.text: Different questions use different kinds of evidence

text.en: A fossil is a preserved trace or remnant of a past organism. An artefact is an object made or modified by people. A find needs context before it supports a claim.

board.text: Fossil: past life · artefact: human modification

text.en: Earth history spans much longer than human history. Geological time gives the setting in which environments and earlier species changed before Homo sapiens appeared.

board.text: Geological time and human history use different scales

text.en: Old drawings sometimes show a single line from one ancestor to modern humans. A branching tree better expresses the evidence that several related human groups existed.
Walking regularly on two legs, changes in hands and teeth, and changes in skulls can be studied from fossils. No single bone tells us the whole story of a population.

board.text: Study several kinds of fossil evidence

text.en: Physical remains depend on what survives. Stone can last after wood, cloth or plant matter has decayed. A collection rich in stone artefacts does not mean people used only stone.
In an undisturbed deposit, a lower layer was usually laid down earlier. Burrows, digging and erosion can disturb layers, so archaeologists check where finds lie.

board.text: Undisturbed layers can show relative age

text.en: Relative dating asks what came first or later. Methods that estimate age in years use other evidence. Write down which kind of dating your claim depends on.

board.text: Relative order differs from an estimated age

text.en: Palaeolithic means Old Stone Age. Sites preserve many kinds of stone artefacts, including larger shaped pieces and flakes. This period covers many places and long spans of time.
Attirampakkam in Tamil Nadu provides examples of early stone artefacts discussed in the textbook. Their find context helps researchers study both the technology and its date.
Gudiyam Cave is another Tamil Nadu example. Stone finds and the setting help researchers ask how ancient people used places in the landscape.

board.text: Gudiyam: finds in a cave setting

text.en: Hunter-gatherers obtained different foods in different settings. Their movements could follow seasons and resources. A camp lets us study one part of a longer seasonal pattern.

board.text: Season and landscape shaped food choices

text.en: A hearth and heat-altered materials can support a claim that fire was used at a site. A piece of burnt material on its own cannot show how a fire started.

board.text: Look for more than one clue to fire use

text.en: Mesolithic means Middle Stone Age in the textbook sequence. Small stone pieces called microliths are important clues in many regional collections.
A microlith could be one part of a larger object. When its handle or binding has decayed, the stone part may be what remains. Archaeologists use wear and context to study likely uses.

board.text: A small stone part can belong to a larger object

text.en: Neolithic sites in several regions show evidence of farming, domesticated animals and settled life. These changes did not begin everywhere at the same time.
Farming could support the storage of food and repeated use of a settlement. Hunting and gathering often continued alongside cultivation and animal keeping.

board.text: New food practices could coexist with earlier ones

text.en: Paiyampalli is a site used in the textbook to study the Neolithic in Tamil Nadu. Artefacts and other remains allow comparisons with sites from the Iron Age.
Pottery can record choices about making, storing and using containers. A vessel’s shape suggests possibilities, while residues and location can provide additional clues.

board.text: Interpret pottery with shape and context

text.en: Chalcolithic refers to a period with copper and stone use in some regions. Bronze Age and Iron Age are also technology labels. Local evidence may show overlap between technologies.

board.text: Technology labels do not imply a universal calendar

text.en: Burial sites such as Adichanallur preserve objects and human remains. Their location and arrangement can help researchers study material culture and past practices.

problem.en: A stone artefact is in one undisturbed layer and a pot fragment is in the layer above it. What can you infer from position alone?

text.en: Check that the layers are undisturbed and compare their positions.

why.en: The lower layer was deposited before the upper layer in this model.

text.en: Separate relative order from an age in years.

why.en: Position gives a sequence. An estimated date needs additional evidence.

prompt.en: A friend says Early humans lived in cities. How will you reply?

points.en: Many Neolithic sites show farming or settled life, with variation across regions.
